reasoning: Quote is verbatim: it is discriminator (3) in the tier-2 'why' text of qb_otherdx_009, and the same false generalization also sits inside option B ('ego-syntonic and acted upon', flagged separately as A1C2-F001), so the finding's framing — that fixing the option alone leaves the explanation still teaching it — matches the source structure. The problem is real under current adult-inpatient practice: command hallucinations are perceptual phenomena experienced as external and are frequently distressing and resisted (Junginger 1990 found compliance in well under half of cases; Chadwick & Birchwood 1994 showed compliance tracks beliefs about the voice, with many patients resisting), so ego-syntonicity is not what separates them from OCD intrusive thoughts — and teaching it as the discriminator invites the unsafe inference that a distressed mother reporting a command hallucination must have 'ego-dystonic' OCD. The replacement teaches the correct discriminators (own-thought vs external percept, intact reality testing, avoidance) and the correct safety rule (any hallucinated command concerning the infant is an emergency regardless of distress), and stays at MS3 level.

Quote is verbatim from the qb_per_004 rationale. The problem is real and not a strained reading: option C in full states that sustained anhedonia and neurovegetative symptoms are 'fully explained by BPD dysregulation and do not warrant evaluation for superimposed major depression' — the precise diagnostic-overshadowing error the keyed answer D names and the item's own evidence anchor ('A BPD diagnosis does not protect a patient from also having a serious mood, psychotic, or medical condition') exists to prevent, in a patient with severe depression and new passive suicidal ideation. Calling C 'the correct clinical description' contradicts the key and, as learner-facing feedback, endorses under-evaluation of a treatable major depressive episode. The replacement correctly reframes C as the error dressed in an accurate opening clause and is level-appropriate for both audiences; its paraphrase of that opening as 'transient and reactive' is if anything more accurate to DSM-5 affective-instability language than the option's 'identity-driven'.

Quote is verbatim from the keyed-best Step 3 option. The omission is real and is not handled anywhere in the surrounding case: substance/alcohol/sedative withdrawal appears in no option, no feedback, and no bias check of delirium_vs_psychosis_001, while Step 2's best answer likewise limits contributors to 'medication and infection'. The vignette's own facts make withdrawal a live etiology — confusion beginning two days post-op with vivid visual hallucinations worse at night is the classic 48-96 h window and phenotype for alcohol/sedative-hypnotic withdrawal delirium, and no substance history is established in either direction. Every standard etiology framework (DSM-5-TR substance-withdrawal delirium, I WATCH DEATH, NICE CG103's cause-identification mandate) includes withdrawal; it is the one delirium cause that is rapidly fatal untreated and whose treatment (benzodiazepines) runs opposite to the sedative-sparing reflex — a reflex the case itself reinforces by rating the sedation option 'harmful'. S1 is defensible on that safety logic. The replacement is a minimal, correct addition at the flagged locus and is squarely MS3-level (post-op day-2 withdrawal is a shelf classic).

Quote is verbatim from the AR-48 Q3 keyed feedback. Checked against the paper: according to PubMed, the Cipriani et al. 2018 Lancet abstract (DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32802-7) reports efficacy ORs from 2.13 (amitriptyline) to 1.37 (reboxetine), and for acceptability 'only agomelatine (OR 0.84) and fluoxetine (0.88) were associated with fewer dropouts than placebo, whereas clomipramine was worse than placebo (1.30)' — amitriptyline's dropout did not differ from placebo and the study nowhere identifies it as having 'the worst side-effect profile' or lowest acceptability, so the deck attributes to the study a result it did not report (the stem's 'limited by the worst side-effect profile (lowest acceptability)' embeds the same false premise, as the finding notes). One nuance that does not rescue the item: in the head-to-head analyses amitriptyline was one of seven drugs in the highest-dropout group (ORs 1.30-2.32), but that neither singles it out as worst nor supports the superlative-as-study-finding. The replacement is accurate — it keeps the true efficacy result, moves amitriptyline's anticholinergic/cardiac burden to a practice-level framing, and correctly states that clomipramine was the acceptability outlier — and is level-appropriate for both audiences.

The quote is faithful, but the claimed problem is not real: the keyed 10% is consistent with the very NMA the stem cites. According to PubMed, the Rodolico et al. 2022 Lancet Psychiatry abstract (DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00437-5) reports that at the primary 12-month timepoint 'ORs compared with treatment as usual ranged from 0.18 (95% CI 0.12-0.27) for family psychoeducation alone to 0.63 (0.42-0.94) for community-based interventions', with family psychoeducation alone superior to the more complex models — and applying OR 0.18 to a 37% usual-care relapse rate yields ~9.6%, i.e., the keyed 10%. The reviewer's premise that the family-intervention literature reports 'roughly a halving' and that 10% is 'far beyond anything reported' is contradicted by the item's own cited source (the ~halving figures belong to the older meta-analyses the basis also cites, not to this NMA), and the reviewer's basis affirmatively mischaracterizes Rodolico 2022. Re-keying to 25% or rewriting to 'roughly halves', as the replacement proposes, would make the material contradict the paper it cites. Caveats — the abstract reports ORs rather than the raw 37%/10% proportions, and the authors grade confidence moderate to very low — could support a different, milder finding about presentation of derived figures, but not this finding's claim that the key is wrong.

The quote is faithful, but the finding's core premise — that the 2025 RCT is untraceable and possibly nonexistent — is false. According to PubMed, the trial exists and matches the deck's description in design, year, comparator, population, and result: Brodsky BS, Galfalvy H, Mann JJ, Grunebaum MF, Stanley B, 'Dialectical Behavior Therapy Versus Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor Treatment for Suicidal Behavior in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial', Am J Psychiatry 2025;182(12):1083-1092 (DOI https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.20240298), which randomized 84 individuals with BPD to 6 months of DBT versus SSRIs with clinical management (SSRI/M) and found significantly fewer suicide-related events, fewer suicide attempts, and lower NSSI counts in the DBT arm during the treatment phase. The quoted feedback ('A 2025 RCT showed that DBT produced significantly fewer suicide-related events than SSRI and clinical management') is therefore an accurate one-line summary of a real, easily locatable trial — a targeted PubMed search on the deck's own descriptors surfaces it immediately — and the Q2 echo is likewise substantiated. The proposed replacement would strip a true, correctly characterized citation, so the finding fails on both the problem and the fix. (Optional polish, not an error: the deck could name the trial, and could note that 12-month follow-up outcomes were comparable between arms.)

Quote is verbatim from the AR-26 Q5 keyed option. The comparator error is real and verified: according to PubMed, the Miklowitz et al. 2007 Arch Gen Psychiatry abstract (DOI https://doi.org/10.1001/archpsyc.64.4.419) shows the 64.4% year-end recovery was significantly higher than the 51.5% of that trial's own randomized comparator, a 3-session collaborative-care psychoeducation control, with intensive psychotherapy delivered 'as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy' — while the antidepressant result (Sachs 2007 NEJM: durable recovery 23.5% vs 27.3% over 26 weeks) came from a separate randomization with a different outcome definition and timeframe. 'Significantly higher than the medication trial' asserts a statistical comparison that was never performed and teaches learners that STEP-BD showed psychotherapy roughly tripling recovery versus medication; the same file's AR-35 Q4 (52% to 64%) demonstrates the deck elsewhere knows the true comparator. The replacement is factually correct and level-appropriate; the stem's cross-trial phrasing would ideally be touched up alongside it, but the corrected option is accurate at the flagged locus and makes nothing wrong.

Quote is verbatim from the AR-26 Q2 distractor feedback. Same verified facts as A3C2-F001: according to PubMed, the Miklowitz 2007 abstract (DOI https://doi.org/10.1001/archpsyc.64.4.419) specifies 293 patients 'treated with protocol pharmacotherapy' randomized to intensive psychotherapy versus collaborative care (3 sessions in 6 weeks), so both arms remained on mood-stabilizer pharmacotherapy and no psychotherapy-versus-medication-alone comparison was ever randomized. 'Compared to medication alone' therefore invents a comparison the companion trial never made and misteaches its design in learner-facing feedback. The replacement states the actual comparator and the adjunctive design accurately and at the right level for both audiences.
